title: The Miller and His Wife

full_text:
Beside a swift mountain brook in the province of Fars stood a watermill where an honest miller and his wife ground wheat into flour for the surrounding villages. They lived in peace and modest comfort, waking with the song of the lark and sleeping soundly to the soothing rhythm of the turning millstone.

One evening, a wealthy caravan merchant, whose mule had gone lame, asked to lodge his goods in the mill for the night. In the miller’s presence, the merchant deposited a heavy iron-bound casket upon the grain bench, saying: 'Guard this casket with your life, for it contains ten thousand gold dinars.'

When the merchant fell asleep, the miller and his wife sat by their oil lamp, staring at the heavy casket. The simple miller whispered: 'Ten thousand dinars! With such a sum, a man could buy a palace in Shiraz, dress in silk, and never touch a dusty sack of flour again.'

His wife sighed: 'And we could have ten servants to bake our bread and wash our linen!'

For the first time in their lives, peace fled from their cottage. Every rustle of the wind sounded like thieves breaking the shutter. The miller paced the floor with a cudgel, terrified that someone would steal the box; his wife tossed on her bed, suspicious that the merchant would accuse them of tampering with the locks. All through the night, they were tormented by fear, greed, and suspicion, unable to close their eyes for a single heartbeat.

At dawn, the merchant arose, paid the miller two silver dirhams for his hospitality, strapped the casket onto his mule, and rode away into the morning mist.

The miller looked at his wife, saw her pale, exhausted face, and then looked at the turning millstone splash in the cool stream.

The miller laughed aloud and embraced her: 'Praise be to heaven! The golden monster has departed! One night under the same roof with ten thousand dinars brought us more misery than forty years of honest labor. Let us grind our wheat in peace, for sweet bread earned with clean hands is worth all the restless gold in the world.'
moral: Contentment with honest toil brings sweet sleep, while greed for unearned gold breeds sleepless suspicion.
